screens.title: Security Automation and Orchestration: an overview
screens.narratorSegment: Today we’re introducing SOAR: Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response. SOAR platforms connect your existing security tools, automate repetitive tasks, and orchestrate multi-step incident responses so analysts can focus on complex investigation. You’ll see why alert fatigue and staffing constraints make SOAR valuable: automation handles routine enrichment and blocking, while orchestration sequences tools to achieve a full response. For example, a simple automation can enrich an alert with reputation data; an orchestration will take that enrichment, query endpoints, adjust firewall rules, and open a ticket when required. This chapter shows you playbook design, example flows for phishing and malicious-process alerts, the common integrations you’ll need, and practical safeguards like approvals and rollback capabilities. By the end, you should be able to explain what a playbook does, design a safe initial workflow, and identify which systems must integrate to make it work. Think about one repetitive task in your current work that could be reduced by automation — we’ll revisit it as a design exercise.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — implementation & safety
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on safe implementation and ongoing maintenance. You will learn to start small: pick repetitive, low-risk tasks like alert enrichment before automating disruptive actions. A concrete example is automating reputation lookups instead of instantly isolating endpoints. Next, you will define and document clear workflows before automating them. Mapping manual steps first prevents surprises when the playbook runs. Third, you will apply a hybrid approach: automate what is safe, and add a human approval step before risky actions like firewall blocks or endpoint isolation. Finally, you will measure effectiveness by tracking mean time to detect and mean time to respond. A common misconception is that automation always reduces risk; in truth, automation can amplify mistakes if playbooks are not tested and rolled back. Each objective ties to a practical milestone: test in non-production, add approvals, and instrument metrics.

screens.title: What is SOAR?
screens.narratorSegment: SOAR is a platform that integrates security tools, automates routine tasks, and orchestrates coordinated incident responses. At its core SOAR does three things: it orchestrates by sequencing actions across systems, it automates individual tasks such as an IOC lookup or quarantine, and it provides incident management so teams can track progress and collaborate. A concrete example is a SIEM alert that triggers a SOAR playbook to enrich the alert with threat intelligence, check endpoint state in an EDR, and create a ticket — all while capturing evidence for analyst review. A common misconception is that SOAR replaces analysts; in fact it augments their capacity by handling low-level work and presenting consolidated data. The result is consistent, repeatable responses, faster containment, and clearer audit trails. When designing or evaluating SOAR, ask which manual tasks are high-volume and low-risk; those are the best candidates for automation, while higher-risk decisions should include human checkpoints. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › What is SOAR?
Definition & components
  • Orchestration: sequencing actions across tools to complete a workflow.
  • Automation: executing single tasks without human input.
  • Incident management: storing incident data and tracking state.
Concrete example
A SIEM alert triggers enrichment, endpoint checks, and ticket creation — automated steps that culminate in analyst review.
Key Takeaway

SOAR is augmentation: it speeds low-risk actions and provides orchestration for complex responses.

Misconception check
Automating everything is dangerous. Instead, map workflows first and add human checks before risky actions like isolation or wide firewall changes.
Automation example
Auto-enrich an alert with TIP data and attach it to the incident.
Orchestration example
Sequence enrichment, EDR query, isolation, ticket creation, and notifications.
Why this matters
SOAR reduces analyst toil, enforces consistency, and shortens mean time to respond, while preserving human judgment for complex decisions.

screens.title: Automation vs Orchestration
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the distinction between automation and orchestration is essential to designing safe playbooks. Automation runs a defined task without human input. A simple automation example is pushing a malicious IP to a firewall block list when reputation crosses a threshold. Orchestration coordinates multiple automations and decision points across tools: a playbook might enrich an alert, query endpoint telemetry, decide if the endpoint is compromised, and then either isolate the endpoint or escalate for review. A common error is treating orchestration as simply stacking automations; orchestration includes conditional logic and sequencing that handles branching outcomes. For instance, if threat intelligence is inconclusive, the orchestration flow should create a low-priority ticket and await analyst review rather than performing disruptive actions. The practical result is safer automation and consistent outcomes. Decide which steps are deterministic and safe to automate, and which require orchestration with clear decision gates and rollback paths. Automation vs Orchestration means automation = single tasks; orchestration = coordinated, conditional sequences that achieve complete responses.. In practical terms, how single tasks differ from coordinated workflows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Automation vs Orchestration
Automation (single tasks)
  • Runs without human input for deterministic steps.
  • Examples: IOC enrichment, quarantine email, push firewall rule.
  • Best for high-volume, low-risk steps.
Common mistake
Automating high-impact actions without approvals can cause outages from false positives.
Orchestration (coordinated workflows)
  • Sequences multiple automated tasks and decision points.
  • Handles branching logic like Yes/No outcomes from threat intel.
  • Example: SIEM trigger → enrich → EDR check → isolate or escalate.
Pro tip
Design orchestration so each branch has explicit rollback and approval steps for risky actions.
Example scenario
A reputation check returns unknown. Automation would only record the lookup. Orchestration then decides: if unknown, create a ticket and tag for analyst review; if malicious, block and isolate automatically only if approval rules are met.

screens.title: Designing a SOAR Playbook
screens.narratorSegment: A well-designed playbook begins with mapping the manual workflow. Start by identifying the trigger (what alert or event starts the flow), then list the data you need to gather, the automated actions to perform, and where a human must decide. For example, in a phishing playbook triggers include a user report or email gateway flag. Steps follow: ingest the email, extract IOCs, query threat intelligence, check endpoints, and quarantine if malicious. Include decision points: is the IOC malicious? If yes, block indicators and isolate endpoints; if no, create a low-priority ticket. Always add logging and evidence collection to preserve context for post-incident review. Test each automated action in a non-production environment and define rollback procedures. A common misconception is that playbooks must be fully automated; instead adopt a hybrid approach where uncertain outcomes prompt human review. The final step is iterating based on metrics: reduce false positives and shorten response time while maintaining safety. Designing a SOAR Playbook means map triggers, data, automated actions, decision gates, human checks, testing, and rollback before automating.. In practical terms, steps to map, automate, and validate an incident workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Designing a SOAR Playbook
Step-by-step process
1. Trigger
Define the alert or user report that starts the playbook.
2. Gather
Collect IOCs, email headers, endpoint telemetry and contextual data.
3. Decide
Add decision logic and thresholds for automated actions versus human review.
4. Act & Review
Execute actions, create tickets, and present results to analysts for closure.
Include evidence capture at each step for audit and investigation.
Test all actions in a safe lab before connecting to production systems.
Define rollback and approval mechanisms for risky actions.
Key Takeaway

Good playbooks map actions and decision points, then iterate based on measured outcomes.

screens.title: Phishing Incident Playbook — step walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a phishing playbook step-by-step using the chapter's sequence. Trigger occurs when a user reports a suspicious email or the gateway flags an attachment. First, ingest the email from the mailbox or quarantine. Next, extract indicators — URLs, domains, sender IPs, and file hashes — and store them in the incident record. Then perform threat intelligence enrichment by querying your TIP to determine whether indicators are known malicious. Following enrichment, query the EDR to check whether any endpoints contacted the indicators or executed the file. Simultaneously check identity providers to see if the sender's account shows suspicious activity. If indicators are malicious, proceed to quarantine the message across mailboxes, push blocks to firewall/proxy, and isolate any compromised endpoint. Automate ticket creation and notifications so the team can track the incident. Finish with an analyst review step to confirm remediation and close the ticket. This flow balances speed with safety and preserves an audit trail for later improvement. Step sequence

  2. Ingest email from mailbox or quarantine.
  3. Extract indicators: URLs, domains, IPs, file hashes.

Enrich: TIP returns reputation scores for IOC lookups.
Contain: Firewall/proxy receives block commands; EDR isolates endpoints.

Which step should include human approval: automated quarantine of a critical user's mailbox, or blocking a public IP used across thousands of services?

screens.title: SOAR Integrations
screens.narratorSegment: SOAR’s value depends on integrations: connectors to SIEM, EDR/XDR, firewalls and proxies, TIPs, vulnerability scanners, identity providers, ticketing systems, and email gateways. Each connector supplies data and accepts actions. For example, SIEM feeds alerts that trigger playbooks and can receive enrichment results. EDR lets SOAR query endpoint state and perform containment like isolation. Firewalls and proxies accept block lists or rules pushed by playbooks. TIPs provide IOC context and reputation data that drive automated decisions. Ticketing systems enable automatic incident creation and lifecycle updates for analysts. Identity providers allow account checks and disabling compromised credentials. Email gateways support ingesting and quarantining messages. Integration complexity varies: robust APIs and maintained connectors make automation reliable; poor integrations increase failure rates. A common misconception is that more integrations are always better — instead prioritize high-value connectors used by your most frequent incidents, and add others as playbooks mature. SOAR Integrations means prioritize reliable, high-value integrations (siem, edr, tip, ticketing) and add others after validating connectors.. screens.title: Playbook for 'Malicious Process Detected'
screens.narratorSegment: Use this hands-on outline to design a playbook for an EDR alert that reports a malicious process. Start with a clear trigger: the EDR alert for Endpoint X. First automated action: query the EDR for process details and recent network connections to collect context. Second, query the TIP for reputation of the process hash or related IPs. Third, evaluate whether the TIP marks the indicators as malicious. If the TIP confirms malicious activity, trigger isolation of the endpoint and create a high-priority ITSM ticket. Include a human review step after isolation so an analyst can validate and perform deeper forensics. If TIP results are inconclusive, create a lower-priority ticket and tag it for manual review. At least three integrations are required: the EDR for detection and isolation, the TIP for enrichment, and the ITSM system for ticketing. Two automated actions are the EDR query and automatic ticket creation; one human review step validates isolation and approves remediation. Test this sequence in a controlled environment before production. Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Malicious Process Playbook
Playbook outline
1. Trigger: EDR alert - "Malicious Process Detected" on Endpoint X.
2. Automated: Query EDR for process details and recent network connections.
3. Automated: Query TIP for reputation of hash/IPs.
4. Decision: Is TIP confirmed malicious?
   IF YES:
     - Isolate Endpoint X via EDR.
     - Create high-priority ticket in ITSM.
     - Notify IR team.
     - Human review and forensic collection.
   IF NO/INCONCLUSIVE:
     - Create low-priority ticket for analyst review.
     - Monitor and collect additional telemetry.
5. End.
Integrations required
  • EDR for detection and isolation.
  • TIP for enrichment and reputation checks.
  • ITSM for ticket creation and tracking.
Pro tip
Automate data collection and ticket creation, but gate isolation with approvals when possible.

screens.title: Risks of Over-Automation
screens.narratorSegment: Automation speeds response, but it can amplify mistakes if not designed carefully. Over-automation is when playbooks perform high-impact actions automatically without adequate checks; a false positive could lead to isolating a critical server or blocking a shared IP used by many services. To avoid this, build safety mechanisms: require approvals for disruptive actions, throttle automatic blocks, and include rollback procedures. fullNarratorScript:
Today we’re introducing SOAR: Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response. SOAR platforms connect your existing security tools, automate repetitive tasks, and orchestrate multi-step incident responses so analysts can focus on complex investigation. You’ll see why alert fatigue and staffing constraints make SOAR valuable: automation handles routine enrichment and blocking, while orchestration sequences tools to achieve a full response. For example, a simple automation can enrich an alert with reputation data; an orchestration will take that enrichment, query endpoints, adjust firewall rules, and open a ticket when required. This chapter shows you playbook design, example flows for phishing and malicious-process alerts, the common integrations you’ll need, and practical safeguards like approvals and rollback capabilities. By the end, you should be able to explain what a playbook does, design a safe initial workflow, and identify which systems must integrate to make it work. Think about one repetitive task in your current work that could be reduced by automation — we’ll revisit it as a design exercise.

These objectives guide your learning. First, you will define SOAR and explain how it reduces alert fatigue by automating enrichment and enabling coordinated actions across tools. As an example, you should be able to describe how a SIEM alert can automatically pull threat intelligence to add context. Second, you will differentiate orchestration from automation: automation runs single tasks without human input, while orchestration sequences tools and automation steps into a full response. A common misconception is thinking orchestration is simply lots of automation; instead orchestration adds decision points and tool coordination. Third, you will design effective playbooks for typical incidents, mapping triggers, decision checks, and where human review should occur. Finally on this screen, you will learn integration basics — which connectors a SOAR needs to work with SIEM, EDR, firewalls, TIPs, and ticketing systems — and why A P I access and reliable connectors matter. Each objective emphasizes practical steps you can test in a lab-ready environment.

This second objectives screen focuses on safe implementation and ongoing maintenance. You will learn to start small: pick repetitive, low-risk tasks like alert enrichment before automating disruptive actions. A concrete example is automating reputation lookups instead of instantly isolating endpoints. Next, you will define and document clear workflows before automating them. Mapping manual steps first prevents surprises when the playbook runs. Third, you will apply a hybrid approach: automate what is safe, and add a human approval step before risky actions like firewall blocks or endpoint isolation. Finally, you will measure effectiveness by tracking mean time to detect and mean time to respond. A common misconception is that automation always reduces risk; in truth, automation can amplify mistakes if playbooks are not tested and rolled back. Each objective ties to a practical milestone: test in non-production, add approvals, and instrument metrics.

SOAR is a platform that integrates security tools, automates routine tasks, and orchestrates coordinated incident responses. At its core SOAR does three things: it orchestrates by sequencing actions across systems, it automates individual tasks such as an IOC lookup or quarantine, and it provides incident management so teams can track progress and collaborate. A concrete example is a SIEM alert that triggers a SOAR playbook to enrich the alert with threat intelligence, check endpoint state in an EDR, and create a ticket — all while capturing evidence for analyst review. A common misconception is that SOAR replaces analysts; in fact it augments their capacity by handling low-level work and presenting consolidated data. The result is consistent, repeatable responses, faster containment, and clearer audit trails. Implementing SOAR successfully relies on a set of practical best practices. Start small: automate enrichment and reporting before attempting disruptive actions. Define clear workflows by documenting manual steps first; this prevents surprises once automated. Test thoroughly in non-production: simulate alerts and verify connector behavior and rollback. Adopt a hybrid approach: combine automation for deterministic tasks with human approvals for ambiguous or high-impact steps. Continuously improve: after incidents, update playbooks to reduce false positives and refine decision thresholds. Measure MTTD and MTTR to show value and prioritize playbook work. Finally, limit blast radius with scoped actions, time-limited rules, and rollback scripts. A common misconception is that automation alone is the improvement — in reality, the value comes from orchestration, good design, and ongoing iteration. These practices reduce risk and ensure SOAR delivers measurable operational gains. Let's summarize three core concepts. First: SOAR integrates tools, automates routine tasks, and orchestrates multi-step incident responses to reduce analyst toil and speed containment. Second: Automation executes individual tasks without human intervention, good for deterministic enrichment and data collection; orchestration sequences those tasks with decision gates and tool coordination for end-to-end response. Third: Playbooks are prescriptive workflows — they must be tested, monitored, and maintained. Common mistakes include automating high-impact actions without approvals and neglecting connector stability. Three additional reminders will help keep your SOAR program healthy. First: prioritize integrations that drive the highest value, such as SIEM, EDR, TIP, and ITSM. Second: maintain playbooks and connectors — treat playbooks like software that needs versioning, testing, and post-incident updates. Third: implement safety controls — approvals, throttles, and rollback mechanisms minimize the blast radius of automated actions. Together these practices ensure automation drives operational improvement without introducing new risks.
